Apple___Apple_scab.appearance: Olive-green to dark brown spots develop on leaves and fruits. Infected leaves may curl or fall early and fruits may become cracked or deformed.
Apple___Apple_scab.cause: A fungal disease mainly caused by Venturia inaequalis. Cool and wet conditions favor infection.
Apple___Apple_scab.recommended_solution: Remove infected leaves and fallen debris, prune trees to improve airflow, and use a locally registered apple-scab fungicide when disease pressure is high.
Apple___Apple_scab.precautions: Avoid prolonged leaf wetness, maintain good spacing and airflow, clean fallen leaves, and prefer resistant apple varieties where available.

Apple___Black_rot.appearance: Leaves may develop purple-edged spots while fruits develop brown to black rotting areas, often with concentric rings.
Apple___Black_rot.cause: Caused mainly by the fungus Botryosphaeria obtusa, which can survive in dead wood and mummified fruits.
Apple___Black_rot.recommended_solution: Remove mummified fruit, dead branches and cankers. Prune infected wood and use locally approved fungicide protection when required.
Apple___Black_rot.precautions: Keep the orchard free of dead wood and damaged fruit, sanitize pruning tools and reduce injuries to branches and fruit.

Apple___Cedar_apple_rust.appearance: Bright yellow-orange spots appear on upper leaf surfaces. Later, tube-like structures may develop on the underside of leaves.
Apple___Cedar_apple_rust.cause: A fungal rust disease caused by Gymnosporangium species that requires both apple and juniper/cedar hosts.
Apple___Cedar_apple_rust.recommended_solution: Remove nearby infected juniper galls when practical and use locally registered protective fungicides during susceptible growth stages.
Apple___Cedar_apple_rust.precautions: Grow resistant apple varieties, increase distance from heavily infected junipers where possible and monitor leaves during wet spring weather.

Apple___healthy.appearance: Leaves appear normally green without characteristic disease spots, lesions or abnormal discoloration.
Apple___healthy.recommended_solution: No treatment is required. Continue normal irrigation, nutrition and orchard management.
Apple___healthy.precautions: Monitor plants regularly, use clean tools, remove diseased debris and maintain balanced irrigation and fertilization.

Blueberry___healthy.appearance: Leaf appears normally green without significant lesions, fungal growth or abnormal spotting.
Blueberry___healthy.recommended_solution: No disease treatment is required. Continue normal plant care.
Blueberry___healthy.precautions: Maintain suitable soil acidity, good drainage, proper airflow and regular disease monitoring.

Cherry_(including_sour)___Powdery_mildew.appearance: White or gray powder-like fungal growth appears on leaves and young shoots. Leaves may curl or become distorted.
Cherry_(including_sour)___Powdery_mildew.cause: A fungal disease favored by humid conditions and dense plant growth.
Cherry_(including_sour)___Powdery_mildew.recommended_solution: Remove heavily infected shoots, improve canopy ventilation and apply a locally registered powdery-mildew fungicide when necessary.
Cherry_(including_sour)___Powdery_mildew.precautions: Avoid excessive nitrogen, maintain spacing and airflow, and regularly remove infected plant material.

Cherry_(including_sour)___healthy.appearance: Leaf shows normal green coloration without obvious fungal growth, spots or lesions.
Cherry_(including_sour)___healthy.precautions: Maintain balanced watering and nutrition, sanitize pruning tools and inspect leaves regularly.

Corn_(maize)___Cercospora_leaf_spot Gray.appearance: Long rectangular gray to tan lesions develop between leaf veins and may merge under severe infection.
Corn_(maize)___Cercospora_leaf_spot Gray.cause: Caused mainly by Cercospora fungi. Warm, humid conditions and infected corn residue increase risk.
Corn_(maize)___Cercospora_leaf_spot Gray.recommended_solution: Rotate with non-host crops, manage infected crop residue and use resistant hybrids. Consider a locally registered fungicide when disease pressure and crop stage justify treatment.
Corn_(maize)___Cercospora_leaf_spot Gray.precautions: Avoid continuous corn where disease is severe, select resistant hybrids and manage residue to reduce fungal survival.

Corn_(maize)___Common_rust_.appearance: Small reddish-brown powdery pustules form on both surfaces of corn leaves.
Corn_(maize)___Common_rust_.cause: Caused by the fungus Puccinia sorghi. Cool to moderate humid conditions favor development.
Corn_(maize)___Common_rust_.recommended_solution: Use resistant corn hybrids. Most mild infections require no treatment, but locally registered fungicides may be considered for susceptible crops under severe pressure.
Corn_(maize)___Common_rust_.precautions: Plant resistant varieties and monitor young plants during cool humid periods.

Corn_(maize)___Northern_Leaf_Blight.appearance: Large cigar-shaped gray-green to tan lesions appear on leaves and may expand significantly.
Corn_(maize)___Northern_Leaf_Blight.cause: Caused by Exserohilum turcicum and favored by humid weather and infected crop residue.
Corn_(maize)___Northern_Leaf_Blight.recommended_solution: Use resistant hybrids, rotate crops, manage infected residue and consider locally registered fungicides when disease risk is high.
Corn_(maize)___Northern_Leaf_Blight.precautions: Avoid repeated susceptible corn crops, maintain residue management and monitor plants during extended wet weather.

Corn_(maize)___healthy.appearance: Leaf appears normally green without characteristic lesions or rust pustules.
Corn_(maize)___healthy.precautions: Maintain proper nutrition, crop rotation, field sanitation and regular scouting.

Grape___Black_rot.appearance: Brown circular leaf spots with darker margins appear. Fruit can shrivel into hard black mummies.
Grape___Black_rot.cause: Caused by the fungus Guignardia bidwellii, which survives in infected berries and plant debris.
Grape___Black_rot.recommended_solution: Remove mummified berries and infected debris, improve airflow and use locally registered fungicides during susceptible growth periods.
Grape___Black_rot.precautions: Prune vines for ventilation, remove infected fruit and avoid leaving diseased material in the vineyard.

Grape___Esca_(Black_Measles).appearance: Leaves can develop interveinal yellow or reddish striping and berries may show dark spotting. Chronic vines may decline.
Grape___Esca_(Black_Measles).cause: Associated with several wood-inhabiting fungi that infect grapevine trunks and pruning wounds.
Grape___Esca_(Black_Measles).recommended_solution: Remove severely affected wood or vines, protect large pruning wounds and maintain vine health. There is no simple curative spray for internal wood infection.
Grape___Esca_(Black_Measles).precautions: Use clean propagation material, sanitize tools and avoid pruning during periods favorable for fungal infection.

Grape___Leaf_blight_(Isariopsis_Leaf_Spo.disease: Grape Leaf Blight / Isariopsis Leaf Spot
Grape___Leaf_blight_(Isariopsis_Leaf_Spo.appearance: Irregular dark brown leaf spots develop and may enlarge, causing premature drying or leaf drop.
Grape___Leaf_blight_(Isariopsis_Leaf_Spo.cause: A fungal leaf-spot disease favored by warm humid conditions.
Grape___Leaf_blight_(Isariopsis_Leaf_Spo.recommended_solution: Remove infected leaves and debris, improve air circulation and use a locally approved grape fungicide if disease becomes severe.
Grape___Leaf_blight_(Isariopsis_Leaf_Spo.precautions: Avoid excessive canopy density, reduce prolonged leaf wetness and maintain vineyard sanitation.

Grape___healthy.appearance: Leaf appears normally green without characteristic spots, mildew or discoloration.
Grape___healthy.precautions: Maintain canopy airflow, sanitation, balanced nutrition and regular scouting.

Orange___Haunglongbing_(Citrus_greening).appearance: Leaves show uneven blotchy yellow mottling. Trees may become weak and fruits can be small, misshapen or remain partly green.
Orange___Haunglongbing_(Citrus_greening).cause: A bacterial disease associated with Candidatus Liberibacter species and spread primarily by citrus psyllids.
Orange___Haunglongbing_(Citrus_greening).recommended_solution: There is currently no reliable cure for an infected tree. Manage the psyllid vector, use certified disease-free planting material and follow local agricultural guidance regarding removal of infected trees.
Orange___Haunglongbing_(Citrus_greening).precautions: Use certified healthy plants, control psyllids using integrated pest management and regularly inspect trees for HLB symptoms.

Peach___Bacterial_spot.appearance: Small water-soaked spots become dark lesions on leaves and fruit. Leaves may develop a shot-hole appearance.
Peach___Bacterial_spot.cause: Caused by the bacterium Xanthomonas arboricola pv. pruni. Wind-driven rain promotes spread.
Peach___Bacterial_spot.recommended_solution: Remove heavily infected material where practical, reduce plant stress and use locally registered bactericide programs when recommended by local agricultural guidance.
Peach___Bacterial_spot.precautions: Grow resistant varieties, avoid unnecessary leaf wetness, maintain balanced nutrition and sanitize tools.

Peach___healthy.appearance: Leaf appears normally green without obvious bacterial or fungal lesions.
Peach___healthy.precautions: Maintain orchard sanitation, balanced irrigation, good airflow and routine monitoring.

Pepper,_bell___Bacterial_spot.appearance: Small water-soaked lesions become dark brown spots on leaves and fruit. Severe infection can cause leaf drop.
Pepper,_bell___Bacterial_spot.cause: Commonly caused by Xanthomonas species and spread by infected seed, transplants and splashing water.
Pepper,_bell___Bacterial_spot.recommended_solution: Remove heavily infected plant material, reduce overhead irrigation and use disease-free seed. Copper-based or other locally registered bactericides may help suppress spread where approved.
Pepper,_bell___Bacterial_spot.precautions: Use clean seed and transplants, rotate crops, disinfect tools and avoid handling plants when foliage is wet.

Pepper,_bell___healthy.appearance: Leaf shows normal green coloration without significant spots or abnormal tissue damage.
Pepper,_bell___healthy.precautions: Use clean planting material, proper watering, crop rotation and regular monitoring.

Potato___Early_blight.appearance: Brown lesions often develop concentric target-like rings, usually beginning on older leaves.
Potato___Early_blight.cause: Primarily caused by Alternaria solani and favored by plant stress, warm temperatures and leaf wetness.
Potato___Early_blight.recommended_solution: Remove infected plant debris, rotate crops, maintain balanced fertility and use locally registered fungicides if disease pressure warrants.
Potato___Early_blight.precautions: Use healthy seed tubers, rotate away from potatoes and tomatoes, avoid excessive plant stress and maintain good field sanitation.

Potato___Late_blight.appearance: Irregular water-soaked dark lesions rapidly enlarge. White fungal-like growth may appear near lesion edges under humid conditions.
Potato___Late_blight.cause: Caused by Phytophthora infestans and favored by cool, wet and humid conditions.
Potato___Late_blight.recommended_solution: Quickly remove badly infected material, destroy volunteer potato plants and use locally registered late-blight fungicides according to local disease warnings and labels.
Potato___Late_blight.precautions: Use certified healthy seed tubers, avoid prolonged leaf wetness, monitor during cool wet weather and remove infected tubers and plant residues.

Potato___healthy.appearance: Leaf appears normally green without characteristic early or late blight lesions.
Potato___healthy.precautions: Use certified seed potatoes, rotate crops, maintain proper irrigation and inspect plants regularly.

Raspberry___healthy.appearance: Leaf appears normally green without significant disease lesions or abnormal discoloration.
Raspberry___healthy.precautions: Maintain good airflow, remove old diseased canes, avoid prolonged leaf wetness and inspect plants regularly.

Soybean___healthy.appearance: Leaf shows normal green coloration without obvious disease symptoms.
Soybean___healthy.precautions: Practice crop rotation, field sanitation, balanced fertilization and routine scouting.

Squash___Powdery_mildew.appearance: White powdery patches appear on leaves and stems and can spread over much of the leaf surface.
Squash___Powdery_mildew.cause: Caused by powdery mildew fungi and favored by humid conditions and dense crop canopies.
Squash___Powdery_mildew.recommended_solution: Remove severely infected leaves, improve airflow and use locally registered powdery-mildew fungicides when needed.
Squash___Powdery_mildew.precautions: Plant resistant varieties, provide adequate spacing and avoid excessive nitrogen fertilization.

Strawberry___Leaf_scorch.appearance: Numerous small purple spots develop on leaves. Spots may merge, giving leaves a scorched or dried appearance.
Strawberry___Leaf_scorch.cause: Primarily caused by the fungus Diplocarpon earlianum and favored by prolonged leaf wetness.
Strawberry___Leaf_scorch.recommended_solution: Remove infected leaves and old plant debris, improve airflow and consider a locally registered fungicide when disease pressure is significant.
Strawberry___Leaf_scorch.precautions: Use clean planting material, avoid excessive overhead irrigation and maintain good field sanitation.

Strawberry___healthy.appearance: Leaves appear normally green without characteristic scorch, lesions or fungal growth.
Strawberry___healthy.precautions: Maintain proper spacing, sanitation and irrigation and inspect plants regularly.

Tomato___Bacterial_spot.appearance: Small dark water-soaked spots appear on leaves and fruit. Severe disease can cause leaf yellowing and defoliation.
Tomato___Bacterial_spot.cause: Caused by several Xanthomonas bacteria and spread through infected seed, transplants, splashing water and tools.
Tomato___Bacterial_spot.recommended_solution: Remove heavily infected material, use disease-free seed and seedlings and reduce overhead irrigation. Locally registered bactericides may be used to suppress spread where recommended.
Tomato___Bacterial_spot.precautions: Rotate crops, disinfect tools, avoid handling wet plants and use clean seed and transplants.

Tomato___Early_blight.appearance: Dark brown spots with concentric target-like rings usually begin on older leaves. Lower leaves may yellow and drop.
Tomato___Early_blight.cause: Primarily caused by Alternaria solani and favored by warm temperatures, moisture and stressed plants.
Tomato___Early_blight.recommended_solution: Remove infected lower leaves and plant debris, mulch to reduce soil splash, rotate crops and use locally registered fungicides when necessary.
Tomato___Early_blight.precautions: Provide adequate spacing, keep foliage dry when possible, use crop rotation and maintain balanced plant nutrition.

Tomato___Late_blight.appearance: Large irregular water-soaked lesions become dark brown. White growth may develop underneath leaves during humid weather.
Tomato___Late_blight.cause: Caused by Phytophthora infestans and spreads rapidly under cool, wet conditions.
Tomato___Late_blight.recommended_solution: Remove and destroy severely infected plants or leaves promptly and use locally registered late-blight fungicides according to agricultural advisories.
Tomato___Late_blight.precautions: Avoid overhead irrigation, improve airflow, remove volunteer tomato and potato plants and monitor closely during cool wet weather.

Tomato___Leaf_Mold.appearance: Yellow patches form on upper leaf surfaces while olive-green to gray mold develops underneath.
Tomato___Leaf_Mold.cause: Caused mainly by Passalora fulva and favored by high humidity, especially in protected cultivation.
Tomato___Leaf_Mold.recommended_solution: Remove infected leaves, improve ventilation and reduce humidity. Use a locally registered fungicide when cultural control is insufficient.
Tomato___Leaf_Mold.precautions: Increase plant spacing, ventilate greenhouses, avoid wetting leaves and use resistant tomato varieties when available.

Tomato___Septoria_leaf_spot.appearance: Many small circular spots with dark borders and light gray centers develop, particularly on lower leaves.
Tomato___Septoria_leaf_spot.cause: Caused by Septoria lycopersici and spread by splashing water from infected plant debris.
Tomato___Septoria_leaf_spot.recommended_solution: Remove infected lower leaves, mulch the soil, improve airflow and use locally registered fungicides if disease continues to spread.
Tomato___Septoria_leaf_spot.precautions: Rotate crops, avoid overhead irrigation, remove tomato debris and control volunteer tomato plants.

Tomato___Spider_mites Two-spotted_spider.appearance: Leaves develop fine yellow stippling or bronzing. Fine webbing may appear when mite populations become high.
Tomato___Spider_mites Two-spotted_spider.cause: Feeding damage caused by two-spotted spider mites, which often increase rapidly in hot dry conditions.
Tomato___Spider_mites Two-spotted_spider.recommended_solution: Remove severely affected leaves, reduce plant stress, use strong water sprays where suitable and conserve natural predators. Use a locally registered miticide only when necessary.
Tomato___Spider_mites Two-spotted_spider.precautions: Monitor leaf undersides regularly, avoid unnecessary broad-spectrum insecticides and prevent plants from becoming excessively drought stressed.

Tomato___Target_Spot.appearance: Brown lesions develop with concentric rings, giving a target-like appearance. Severe infections may cause leaf drop.
Tomato___Target_Spot.cause: Commonly associated with Corynespora cassiicola and favored by warm humid weather.
Tomato___Target_Spot.recommended_solution: Remove infected debris, improve airflow, avoid prolonged leaf wetness and use a locally registered fungicide if disease becomes severe.
Tomato___Target_Spot.precautions: Rotate crops, maintain adequate spacing and avoid excessive overhead irrigation.

Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.appearance: Young leaves curl upward, become yellow and smaller, while plants may become stunted and produce fewer fruits.
Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.cause: A viral disease primarily transmitted by whiteflies.
Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.recommended_solution: There is no curative treatment for an infected plant. Remove severely infected plants and manage whitefly populations using integrated pest management.
Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.precautions: Use virus-resistant tomato varieties, control weeds that can host whiteflies, use healthy seedlings and monitor whitefly populations.

Tomato___Tomato_mosaic_virus.appearance: Leaves show light and dark green mosaic patterns and may become distorted or narrowed. Plant growth may be reduced.
Tomato___Tomato_mosaic_virus.cause: A highly stable virus spread through infected plant material, seed contamination and mechanical contact.
Tomato___Tomato_mosaic_virus.recommended_solution: There is no cure for infected plants. Remove infected plants, disinfect tools and avoid handling healthy plants immediately after infected plants.
Tomato___Tomato_mosaic_virus.precautions: Use certified healthy seed, sanitize hands and tools, remove infected plant debris and avoid tobacco contamination around tomato plants.

Tomato___healthy.appearance: Leaf appears normally green without characteristic fungal, bacterial, viral or mite damage.
Tomato___healthy.precautions: Maintain proper watering, balanced nutrition, field sanitation, airflow and regular pest and disease monitoring.
